extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary history and medieval/heroic poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for composing and evaluating chivalrous/heroic (Teutonic/medieval) poetry and related lyric forms (hymns, heroic lays), focusing on form, language, theme, and performative function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warm expression of feeling for hymns
rubrics_metrics.description: In hymns and songs the warm expression of feeling is alone sufficient to constitute excellence; Christian hymn-writers had the Psalms as exemplary models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For religious lyric (hymn) forms, prioritize sincere emotional expression over technical novelty; follow the intensity and directness of the Psalms. Formal complexity is less important than devotional warmth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must suit subject (avoid mismatched classical forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of composition borrowed from the ancient poets was little adapted for describing the whole system of Christianity; ambitious attempts using those forms produced centos — metrically correct and elevated in language but lacking life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mechanically impose inherited classical epic forms on subjects for which they are unsuited. Choose or adapt forms that can carry the subject's substantive demands; otherwise the result risks being an elegant but lifeless pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life and spirit over mere metrical elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrical arrangement and elevated language alone do not make poetry; what matters is life and spirit — the living impulse and emotional vitality behind the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing poetry, prioritize vitality, imaginative engagement, and emotional truth. Avoid compositions that are technically polished but emotionally inert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and coherence of mythic/narrative system
rubrics_metrics.description: The northern (Scandinavian) theology and poetry are notable for their unity and entire consistency — the whole often reads as one connected progressive poem or tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a coherent overarching structure or mythic logic in long narrative poems; propagating prophecies, consistent themes, and a teleological arc strengthens the work's power and distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic teleology and foreseen catastrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: A central organizing interest in Teutonic poetry is the foretelling of a final catastrophe (the decline of the heroic world); prophetic structure and the expectation of doom (e.g., the death of Balder) give the poetry its tragic force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embedding a sense of destiny or impending catastrophe can heighten dramatic tension and thematic depth. Use prophecy, foreshadowing, and inexorable fate to give large-scale narrative poems a tragic coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plan and successive, naturally linked pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic poems like the Nibelungen-lied are distinguished by unity of plan: a series of successive pictures, each following naturally from the last, producing a cohesive whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure long poems as a sequence of interlinked episodes that advance the central theme or plot. Each scene should connect logically and emotionally to the next, avoiding disjointedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boldness and simplicity; economy (disregard of superfluities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief characteristics of certain heroic poems are boldness and simplicity, and a total disregard of all superfluities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor direct, forceful diction and omit unnecessary ornament. Clarity and compression can produce greater impact than elaborate embellishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid unfolding of incident and dramatic representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Skilful unfolding of incidents and almost dramatic vividness of representation (a Homeric quality) are major virtues; even when a simpler mode is chosen, effective incident unfolding remains crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose scenes with attention to dramatic progression and vivid, concrete detail so that events unfold naturally and powerfully in the reader's imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lively, strong, flexible language; avoid affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: At its best, the language of heroic poetry displays liveliness, strength, and flexibility; later periods fell into affectation, hardness, and perplexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use idiom and diction that feel energetic and adaptable to the poem's needs. Beware of ornamental or convoluted language that reduces clarity and vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero as archetype embodying splendour and decline
rubrics_metrics.description: Central heroes are often youthful figures invested with beauty, magnanimity, and victory who nevertheless are destined to early death; they personify both the splendour and the decline of the heroic world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create protagonists who function simultaneously as individual characters and as symbolic embodiments of wider cultural or epochal themes; their arc should reflect larger transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenderness and pathos in depictions of death
rubrics_metrics.description: The death of heroes in German heroic poetry is depicted with solemnity, stillness, and exquisite touches of tenderness—often more touching than comparable scenes elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying death, allow space for quiet, tender detail and emotional restraint; subtle pathos can be more affecting than melodrama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety: depict both joyful and sorrowful aspects of life
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic poems often encompass a broad range of human experience — both joyous festivities and bloody combats, love and tears — giving the work emotional and thematic breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance scenes of revelry, love, and domestic feeling with scenes of conflict and tragedy to produce a richer, more resonant poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performative, recitable quality (inspiriting function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic songs were used to inspirite soldiers before battle and belonged to oral traditions; their performative potency was central to their social function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with attention to sound, cadence, and lines that can be recited or sung; consider the oral/performance context and how the poem will affect listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, impressive openings naming proper subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective heroic poems open with short, impressive statements that announce proper subjects (e.g., fall of nations, contests of heroes) directly and memorably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a compact, striking statement of theme or subject to orient the audience immediately and establish tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention and adaptation of traditional forms for language/versification
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian poets often copied and adopted the forms of preceding heroic poems, which supplied valuable information about contemporary language and versification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working within a traditional genre, study and borrow its formal properties (meter, diction, stanzaic patterns) where they help convey authenticity, but adapt them to new subjects as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral-tradition qualities should inform written forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Many heroic poems were originally oral and recited by bards; that oral character (repetition, formulaic phrase, directness) shaped their style and function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing in a heroic/epic vein, incorporate oral qualities—formulaic phrases, memorable refrains, rhythmic propulsion—to preserve immediacy and communal resonance.
